locator.quote: so it gives no positive-budget separation here.

feedback.feedback: The small board’s lack of asymptotic hardness is now honestly stated. I would retain this boundary even though it interrupts the narrative slightly: a worked finite example can teach an operation without witnessing the theorem’s quantitative separation.
feedback.why_it_matters: Students often treat a tiny illustrated construction as numerical evidence for its eventual asymptotic cost.
feedback.advice: Keep the boundary once at the first consequential use, and keep the later planted picture explicitly schematic about hardness.

locator.section: 2. One column, then four — attribution paragraph
locator.quote: They used about $10\log n$ copies; we take $r=20\log_2m$.

feedback.feedback: Between the winning definition and the concrete four-column board, this long paragraph handles predecessor credit, two address lengths, a direct-product probability, a union bound, a polynomial-size array and an alphabet objection. Every topic is legitimate, but their accumulation delays the operation students are waiting to try.
feedback.why_it_matters: The reader must carry an untested abstract definition while encountering several arguments whose purpose becomes clear only later.
feedback.advice: Keep concise attribution at the construction. Place the address-length calculation at the lower-bound union and the alphabet comparison with the historical discussion, preserving both explanations rather than adding another summary.

locator.section: 2. One column, then four — distinct indices
locator.quote: These are different indices, even though both have length two in our small example.

feedback.feedback: The address/pointer distinction is well placed and should survive further shortening. The equal lengths in the toy would otherwise hide an important difference in what the two words select.
feedback.why_it_matters: Confusing cell selection with row selection makes both the comparison algorithm and the planted-cell reduction impossible to reconstruct.
feedback.advice: Retain the role distinction and the different labels r and ell in the general diagram.

locator.quote: The strings of all columns, and the address inputs and cells of a winning column

feedback.feedback: Figure 1 is coherent and unclipped, but at normal page size its blue address-input text and the two-line cell description are substantially smaller than the surrounding prose. Those are precisely the labels a lecturer would point at to explain the two kinds of addressing.
feedback.why_it_matters: The architecture is visible before the key labels are comfortably readable, so students must alternate between figure and caption to identify each operation.
feedback.advice: Enlarge those labels and allow more vertical space or fewer repeated miniature cells. Do not reduce the figure to save a page; keep the operation labels readable.

locator.section: 2. One column, then four — unique winner
locator.quote: a pointer from one winner would have to find a zero in the all-one string of another.

feedback.feedback: This one-sentence uniqueness proof is ideal for a classroom. It uses the definition just given, does not hide a lemma, and identifies the exact role of the outward pointers.
feedback.why_it_matters: Uniqueness can otherwise look like a mysterious property of the Forrelation inputs rather than an elementary property of the certificate geometry.
feedback.advice: Keep it close to the four clauses; ask students to identify which clauses were used if a brief comprehension check is needed.

locator.section: 2. One column, then four — linked finite circuit
locator.quote: That checker tests the circuit on all 256 inputs

feedback.feedback: The repaired warning about the checker’s different board is mathematically responsible, but it interrupts the first explanation of transcripts with a second pair of unshown positive and negative strings. For classroom use I would explain the gate test first and treat the comparison of example editions as an optional source note.
feedback.why_it_matters: A reader interested in the mechanism has to track a source-checking discrepancy before seeing why a local gate check works.
feedback.advice: Keep a short accurate notice that the linked checker uses a different board, and put the detailed amplitude comparison at the linked destination or in a compact note after the worked gate test. Do not revert to claiming the boards are identical.

locator.section: 2. One column, then four — output tests
locator.quote: Finally, there are $2r$ output tests

feedback.feedback: A student can reasonably ask why an output gate is checked once among the S gate equations and again among the 2r output tests. The distinction is recoverable from the surrounding text and is explicit in the record, but it deserves one local sentence where K is assembled.
feedback.why_it_matters: Without that distinction, the extra 2r looks like double counting or a removable redundancy.
feedback.advice: Explain that a gate equation checks consistency with its predecessors, whereas the output test checks the meaning required of that value: domain membership or agreement with the proposed address.

locator.section: 2. One column, then four — actual gate example
locator.quote: the actual input bit $x_7=0$

feedback.feedback: The example now distinguishes actual input wires from stored transcript wires. It teaches an executable three-query test, not just a slogan about local verification.
feedback.why_it_matters: This is what lets a reader understand why a false transcript cannot simply invent mutually consistent input values.
feedback.advice: Preserve the actual gate example through the next prose pass; if its indexing is simplified, keep the distinction between queried input and alleged gate output.

locator.section: 2. One column, then four — circuit consistency task
locator.quote: A false transcript cannot satisfy every gate equation, by the induction above.

feedback.feedback: Question 1 tests domain and address outputs while every gate equation is true. It therefore does not test whether students understand the induction that makes local consistency meaningful. That is a separate promised operation from counting domain failures.
feedback.why_it_matters: A student can answer the existing question correctly while still thinking the verifier trusts a chain of mutually supporting false gate values.
feedback.advice: Offer a short changed-transcript follow-up using the already introduced gates: change a proposed predecessor and a later output, then ask where the earliest false gate must be caught. Keep it as an application of the existing argument.

locator.quote: On the changed board, which of column $2$'s tests fail

feedback.feedback: The question is clear when read immediately, but “the changed board” is a fragile assignment reference because the paper soon introduces several different changed boards. The task needs a stable locator when quoted on a problem sheet or revisited after Section 4.
feedback.why_it_matters: Students can accidentally import the dominant-nonwinner or cyclic-board mutation and then obtain different failing tests.
feedback.advice: Name this as the domain-bit change or identify the two swapped strings in the question. A short label is enough; do not repeat the solution.

locator.section: 2. One column, then four — historical composition
locator.quote: a partial function $g$ on $n$ bits is first composed with AND-OR on $n^2$ bits.

feedback.feedback: For a reader who has only seen composition of ordinary functions, it is not yet explicit that there are n separate AND-OR blocks, one producing each input bit of g. The following n-by-n picture describes one block, while the total composed input has n such blocks.
feedback.why_it_matters: The ensuing certificate and cost multiplication can be assigned to the wrong object.
feedback.advice: Identify the n inner copies and the n outputs fed to g before discussing one block’s certificates. This is a short clarification, not a request to reproduce the predecessor construction.

locator.section: 2. One column, then four — historical randomized bound
locator.quote: this recipe has randomized lower bound $R(g)n^2$

feedback.feedback: The historical lower-bound product is cited, but the prose can make it sound like ordinary multiplication of two query costs. A randomized composition lower bound is an inherited result, not a rule students may apply to any two problems.
feedback.why_it_matters: The passage risks teaching a general lower-bound shortcut that the rest of this article carefully avoids.
feedback.advice: Identify this as the bound supplied by the cited cheat-sheet/composition argument and distinguish it from the elementary certificate count immediately before it.

locator.section: 3. The general partial function — three facts
locator.quote: The construction uses $k$-fold Forrelation through three facts

feedback.feedback: This is a good interface for a lecture. The cheap decoder, exact small circuit and classical hardness have different jobs, and the section does not ask a newcomer to reproduce the analytic Forrelation lower bound in order to follow the total-function construction.
feedback.why_it_matters: The separation between an imported theorem and the argument being taught keeps the scope achievable.
feedback.advice: Keep the three roles visible and test students on which later proof consumes each one.

locator.section: 3. The general partial function — concentration input
locator.quote: by a Chernoff bound

feedback.feedback: The declared elementary probability background does not necessarily include Chernoff bounds. The section gives a specific repetition count and calls this inequality by name without saying whether the reader is expected to derive it or accept it.
feedback.why_it_matters: A student may stop to verify the constant 16 even though the later proof only needs the logarithmic error dependence and the all-input cap.
feedback.advice: State the concentration estimate as a supplied elementary tool, or put its scalar form in a short optional note. Keep its role and hypotheses; do not expand the main route into a concentration chapter.

locator.section: 3. The general partial function — quantitative circuit bound
locator.quote: Its near-linear size matters because the verifier will search $rS$ gate tests.

feedback.feedback: This sentence earns the otherwise forbidding circuit-size display. It tells the class why the circuit may be expensive to evaluate but still useful to verify by searching local equations.
feedback.why_it_matters: Without the stated use, S can look like implementation bookkeeping rather than one of the two mechanisms that determine the quantum exponent.
feedback.advice: Retain it beside the bound and recall that specific role when K is used in verification.

locator.section: 3. The general partial function — total length
locator.quote: the total input length is polynomial in $m$, although much larger than $m$.

feedback.feedback: This distinction is now explicit, but it is a useful point for a classroom comprehension question: the displayed fourth power compares two query measures of the same input, not either measure with the number m of columns.
feedback.why_it_matters: Students familiar with standard input-size complexity may continue to report Q as the square root of the complete input length.
feedback.advice: Use a one-sentence check asking which symbol denotes the actual input length and which parameter controls the displayed query bounds; do not add another asymptotic derivation.

locator.quote: a direct search costs too much.

feedback.feedback: The failed nested-Grover calculation gives the tournament an intelligible purpose. I would use it as the opening blackboard calculation for this part of a course.
feedback.why_it_matters: It makes the new algorithm solve a specific cost problem rather than arrive as unexplained machinery.
feedback.advice: Keep the two square-root factors and the explanation that final verification is performed only on a short list.

locator.quote: Because the decoded labels are never erased, branches with different labels stay orthogonal

feedback.feedback: The paragraph states the right preservation argument, but for the advertised non-quantum students it compresses deferred measurement, reversible classical control, retained histories and marginal probabilities into a single verbal account. I can teach it, but I cannot infer that students can reconstruct the operation just because every necessary phrase is present.
feedback.why_it_matters: This is the first genuinely new implementation bridge in the article, and it is needed again when amplification is inverted.
feedback.advice: Show one small input/output register transformation for a comparison, with the decoded label and success bit retained, then identify what is measured and what is inverted. Reuse that display in sampling rather than add another explanatory paragraph.

locator.quote: Comparisons on the board with cycled loser pointers.

feedback.feedback: The tournament drawing is readable, but the current PDF still gives it a largely empty page 9 between the comparison discussion and the weight analysis. This is a known residual rather than a newly missing figure. In a handout it makes a short supporting picture feel like a new chapter.
feedback.why_it_matters: The reader must turn away from the argument and then recover the active board and purpose of the diagram on the next page.
feedback.advice: Adjust float placement so the readable diagram sits with its comparison or first-weight calculation. Preserve label size; the repair is page flow, not shrinking the figure.

locator.quote: The rows show the winning pointers

feedback.feedback: The repaired caption correctly says that the displayed pointer rows are the winning directions while the prose lists the reverse directions that were changed. A classroom reader still has to reconcile those two descriptions to check the cycle.
feedback.why_it_matters: The figure visibly asserts the cycle, but does not quite make checking the three decisive comparisons a single local operation.
feedback.advice: In the existing pointer rows, indicate the corresponding reverse target values compactly, or point explicitly to the three changed reverse pointers beside the figure. Do not replace the explanation with a prose table.

locator.quote: The weights are defined from the unknown probabilities $a_{ij}$; the algorithm never computes or estimates them.

feedback.feedback: This sentence prevents the most tempting implementation misconception. The weights are an analytical description of the experiment, and the later product-preparation formula shows how the law appears without numerical access to them.
feedback.why_it_matters: If students think the quantum algorithm first computes the weights, they will miss both the query saving and the point of coherent comparisons.
feedback.advice: Preserve it and make this distinction one of the oral teach-back criteria.

locator.quote: The sampler does not choose uniformly among positive weights.

feedback.feedback: The new fractional example is the right repair, but every numbered tournament calculation still uses only zero and one weights. As a lecturer I cannot use Question 2 to check that students learned the feature this example was added to teach.
feedback.why_it_matters: Correct execution of the deterministic board can coexist with the mistaken rule “choose uniformly among surviving columns.”
feedback.advice: Extend an existing task with one continuation of the already supplied abstract fractional matrix, asking for joint success masses and normalized label probabilities. State that it remains an abstract matrix, not a claimed new board realization.

locator.quote: A phase flip on the success flag and a reflection about the prepared state give a rotation

feedback.feedback: This is a geometric proof without a picture or displayed reflection matrix. Students with linear algebra can follow it, but a lecturer must supply the two axes and two reflections before the sine formula feels derived rather than quoted.
feedback.why_it_matters: The formula carries the important successful-law invariant; treating the rotation as a black box weakens that explanation.
feedback.advice: Use a small two-dimensional geometric sketch or the existing record’s two-by-two transformation, labelled by the full-workspace good and bad states. Choose one representation, not both by default.

locator.quote: The coefficient of $g$ changes, but the relative label probabilities inside $g$ do not.

feedback.feedback: This is the exact property the sampler needs, and it is now explained rather than merely asserted. The warning that g contains all retained workspace is essential to the claim.
feedback.why_it_matters: Increasing the probability of a success flag alone would not establish the correct pivot law.
feedback.advice: Preserve both the invariant and the whole-workspace qualification; a shorter paraphrase must still say what conditional distribution is unchanged.

locator.quote: too many iterations can rotate past the success direction.

feedback.feedback: The text names overshoot, but the exercises exhibit a stationary p=1/2 case and a p=1/4 case that becomes perfect after one iteration. They do not ask the reader to see the failure of monotone improvement.
feedback.why_it_matters: Students may retain “one iteration helps” as their operational rule and overlook why a bounded randomized count is necessary.
feedback.advice: After the existing p=1/4 calculation, ask what a second Grover iteration would do. This uses the same data and sine formula, so it tests the warning without introducing another example.

locator.section: 4. The quantum algorithm — bounded amplification destination
locator.quote: gives the trial counts.

feedback.feedback: The linked anchor upper-amplification-proof starts near the end of record §5.1, after M, N and the randomized trial construction were introduced. A student following this sentence for the promised trial counts arrives at a proof that already uses them.
feedback.why_it_matters: A technically valid link can still require searching upward through several paragraphs before the advertised material is available.
feedback.advice: Link the trial-count invitation to upper-grover-trial, or to the start of §5.1 with an explicit local destination; retain a separate link to the final correctness proof if useful.

locator.section: 4. The quantum algorithm — query units in amplification
locator.quote: What does one Grover iteration do here?

feedback.feedback: This question checks the success probability, but a student coming from ordinary search may equate one Grover iteration with one input query. Here an iteration invokes the whole preparation and its inverse, whose cost includes comparisons.
feedback.why_it_matters: The same word “iteration” refers to a much more expensive unit than a single oracle call in the standard four-item search exercise.
feedback.advice: Ask the student to identify the unit being counted, or add a brief reminder beside the exercise that an iteration is not one bit query in this construction.

locator.quote: Here the search's success flag means **a violation was found**.

feedback.feedback: This explicit reversal of the everyday meaning of success is necessary and well positioned. It makes acceptance of a valid certificate compatible with certain failure of the violation search.
feedback.why_it_matters: Without it, a student can reverse the final Boolean output while following all the probability formulas correctly.
feedback.advice: Keep the bold local definition and use the domain-bit example to ask which flag is set, without adding a new flag vocabulary throughout the paper.

locator.quote: Decoder errors within comparisons are already included in the actual probabilities $a_{ij}$.

feedback.feedback: This sentence is important but currently functions as a final warning after the error totals. A student doing the count independently is likely to add decoder errors again because earlier amplification and verification errors were listed separately.
feedback.why_it_matters: Double counting is harmless for some loose estimates but obscures what the weighted analysis actually proves.
feedback.advice: Make the existing distinction a short question: which errors are part of the comparison law and which are additional failures of the algorithm? Require students to point to the corresponding terms.

locator.quote: The exponent six is an artefact of this loose count.

feedback.feedback: The section spends several paragraphs on a deliberately loose logarithmic power after proving the novel search mechanism. The explanation is correct, but for a course I would mark the exact loose exponent as a second-pass calculation rather than let it compete with the square-root idea.
feedback.why_it_matters: Students may remember the sixth power of a logarithm more clearly than why only a short list is verified.
feedback.advice: Keep the complete cost factors accessible, identify the count as a check of the stated quantitative theorem, and let the main reading route retain the square-root plus polylogarithmic conclusion.

locator.section: 5. The classical lower bound — hard law
locator.quote: one distribution defeats **all** capped deterministic trees

feedback.feedback: This is an effective explanation of why minimax is used. It gives the quantifier exchange a mathematical job before the proof starts sampling independent address inputs.
feedback.why_it_matters: A different adverse distribution for each algorithm would not support the single planted-pair construction.
feedback.advice: Keep it. A lecturer may accept the stated finite minimax theorem without adding a new game-theory detour.

locator.section: 5. The classical lower bound — Figure 4 and proof flow
locator.quote: The planted pair on the four-column board

feedback.feedback: In the current PDF, Figure 4 occupies the top of page 14 and separates the middle of the erased-zero argument from its continuation (“therefore finds its zero…”). The figure is needed for the pair construction, but this float placement interrupts a different, conditional-probability proof.
feedback.why_it_matters: Students must retain the full transcript-prefix conditioning across a page turn and an unrelated large visual.
feedback.advice: Place the pair figure immediately with the pair definition, before the deterministic-tree comparison, or otherwise keep the erased-zero paragraph together. Preserve its current readable size.

locator.section: 5. The classical lower bound — realized picture
locator.quote: the address inputs are now samples from $\mu$

feedback.feedback: The reset from the earlier board is stated, which is good. The figure also shows the specific address 10, so I would say explicitly that this is one displayed realization with that address, not a statement that sampling from the hard law always produces it.
feedback.why_it_matters: A student learning distributional lower bounds may conflate the law with the one outcome drawn for illustration.
feedback.advice: Keep the hidden-from-the-algorithm warning and identify the displayed address as the selected sample’s realization. No concrete hard-law calculation at m=4 is required.

locator.section: 5. The classical lower bound — erased-zero exercise
locator.quote: With two fixed positions queried per column

feedback.feedback: Question 3 is useful arithmetic practice, but it avoids the adaptive feature that makes the preceding erased-zero proof subtle. Both parts use a fixed set of queried positions, so success on this exercise is weak evidence that a student understands conditioning on the complete transcript prefix.
feedback.why_it_matters: The hard step is retaining uniformity among unread positions after adaptive observations, not calculating a binomial no-hit probability.
feedback.advice: Add a short follow-up asking which identity still holds when later queries depend on earlier answers and why the planted column must remain independent. Do not require a new sharp adaptive search bound.

locator.section: 5. The classical lower bound — whole-run lightness
locator.quote: Call a column **heavy** if the dummy run makes more than $L$ queries

feedback.feedback: At the first definition, explicitly say “complete dummy run.” The following sentence immediately fixes a query time j, and a student can then silently read “light” as light up to time j. Answer 4 eventually explains the future-query issue, but the definition should guard it before the exercise.
feedback.why_it_matters: The event used by the simulator inclusion is not the same as being cheap only at the instant of visiting the cell.
feedback.advice: Add the scope word at the definition and retain the later counterexample in Answer 4. This is a clarification of the existing event, not a new requirement.

locator.section: 5. The classical lower bound — counterexample density
locator.quote: Both hypotheses are needed.

feedback.feedback: The direct-product statement is followed by a pooled-budget AND example, an XOR side-information example, a dense optional proof, a different promised-AND example and then the simulator’s fair-XOR example. Each is useful, but a lecturer has to keep announcing which law and task are active.
feedback.why_it_matters: The main planted-cell question disappears for several changes of miniature problem, even though the prose defines each change correctly.
feedback.advice: Keep the two indispensable guards on the main reduction, and mark a clear optional route through the supplier proof and its auxiliary examples. Use brief role labels when returning to the planted construction; do not delete a hypothesis explanation merely to reduce example count.

locator.section: 5. The classical lower bound — optional proof
locator.quote: Let $q_h(\tau)$ count the queries

feedback.feedback: The optional proof introduces the transcript rectangle, conditional laws, remaining budgets and an optimization value before giving the two-AND calculation. For students, the numeric calculation would provide a more concrete meaning for “best remaining success” if it preceded the full V_h notation.
feedback.why_it_matters: The proof is logically complete but the reader must first understand an abstract dynamic program to discover what it is measuring.
feedback.advice: Use the existing AND calculation to introduce the value, then generalize; preserve the rectangle justification and leaf bound rather than replacing them with intuition.

locator.section: 5. The classical lower bound — proof-box paragraphs
locator.quote: Fix the coins and side information.

feedback.feedback: The optional proof is set as two very dense paragraphs in the shaded box on page 15. Those paragraphs each do several different jobs: product conditioning, the value update, the example, the product supermartingale and the leaf comparison.
feedback.why_it_matters: The visual label “optional” makes skipping easy, but does not make the chosen proof route teachable for a student who actually reads it.
feedback.advice: Break the full-width proof at its mathematical changes of task, leaving the displayed conditional-value inequality with its explanation. No table or extra status headings are needed.

locator.section: 5. The classical lower bound — simulator side information
locator.quote: A simulator is given everything except the address inputs of column $i$

feedback.feedback: The simulator’s stronger information is stated precisely, but students may wonder why revealing all other fields for free does not cheat. The sentence supplies the independence fact without quite explaining the reduction’s permission to give away that information.
feedback.why_it_matters: A learner can mistake a proof-only predictor for an implementation of the original G-query algorithm and reject the reduction for the wrong reason.
feedback.advice: Explain that the direct-product bound is designed to remain valid with this independent side information, so defeating it with the more informed simulator would still be impossible. Keep the original algorithm’s global cap distinct.

locator.section: 5. The classical lower bound — three budgets
locator.quote: Three budgets are in play.

feedback.feedback: The paragraph successfully distinguishes the global cap, total target-column cap and separate per-instance caps. It also explains the implication rather than relying on the shared letter L.
feedback.why_it_matters: This is the precise interface that makes the direct-product result applicable to a truncated original run.
feedback.advice: Retain the entire implication. A concise numeric exercise could test it, but the present explanation should not be compressed to “apply the direct product.”

locator.section: 5. The classical lower bound — simulator toy indexing
locator.quote: numbers columns from $0$.

feedback.feedback: The indexing reset is correctly disclosed, but the target “column 1” is now the second column while it was the first column and winner in the earlier board. A student reusing the visual memory of Figure 2 must inhibit it deliberately.
feedback.why_it_matters: This is avoidable representational work at the hardest point of the classical proof.
feedback.advice: Call it the second column, labelled 1 in the linked example, at its first use. Preserve the supplied record’s indexing rather than silently renumbering the source.

locator.section: 5. The classical lower bound — Question 4 stopping condition
locator.quote: if the run stops after the cell query?

feedback.feedback: The stopping clause makes the question well posed, and its answer correctly explains that a later read of c would make the complete run heavy. That last distinction is currently supplied only after the student answers the easier stopped-run case.
feedback.why_it_matters: The exercise’s most valuable generalization is revealed as a comment instead of being something the student must decide.
feedback.advice: Ask the later-query variant as an explicit second part before exposing the answer, while keeping the stopped-run calculation as initial practice.

locator.section: 5. The classical lower bound — event inclusion
locator.quote: The implication goes one way

feedback.feedback: This is a successful explanation of the lower bound’s delicate reduction. The 1/8 versus 1/4 XOR calculation shows why a lucky default only enlarges the predictor’s success event, rather than needing to be ruled out.
feedback.why_it_matters: It makes the inequality direction operational and avoids the invalid conditional-on-being-cheap proof.
feedback.advice: Keep both the set-inclusion explanation and the default-success example; they are the central teaching payoff of this section.

locator.section: 5. The classical lower bound — no extra column union
locator.quote: There is no extra factor of $m$.

feedback.feedback: The displayed average proves the cancellation correctly. For a classroom reader, one more identification of the event would help: the proof asks about the independently selected planted column, not whether any column’s true cell is ever visited.
feedback.why_it_matters: The difference between those two questions explains why a union over all columns would be the wrong calculation.
feedback.advice: Tie the sentence to that event distinction or use it as a one-line oral question; do not add another bound.

locator.quote: Both quantities tend to infinity for fixed $k$

feedback.feedback: The floor repair is correct. The opening paragraph nevertheless repeats “so” across three consecutive sentences while handling two separate floors and a threshold. In lecture notes this routine calculation deserves a more economical rhythm.
feedback.why_it_matters: The reader has just reached the conceptual payoff and must pause for low-level arithmetic that no longer carries a new idea.
feedback.advice: Retain the two eventual-growth justifications, but combine their shared reason and move promptly to the strict exponent gap. Do not restore the old insufficient numerical threshold.

locator.quote: What does $k=4$ prove about $\alpha_{\rm tot}$?

feedback.feedback: Question 5 now tests exactly the distinction it ought to test: an infimum lower bound does not itself refute the endpoint inequality. Its answer is correct, and k=5 is a simple witness for excluding the endpoint 3.5.
feedback.why_it_matters: This is a meaningful change of use, not just a numerical substitution in a formula.
feedback.advice: Preserve this corrected question and answer. The next pass should not re-raise the old endpoint error.

locator.quote: Before leaving the argument, try to explain it using the two examples.

feedback.feedback: The closing questions are the best test of the stated teaching goal, but unlike the numbered questions they have no separate answer criteria. A student can repeat “quantum interference and hidden certificates” and feel finished without explaining the two cost mechanisms or the order of quantifiers.
feedback.why_it_matters: The article’s final promise is explanatory reconstruction, while the scored tasks mostly verify local arithmetic and cases.
feedback.advice: Give a short separate checklist for a successful teach-back: the two changed locations, the joint capped-prediction event, weight sampling without estimating weights, retained-list verification, and the fixed-k exponent calculation. This is assessment guidance, not a replacement conclusion.

locator.section: 7. The statement in Lean — entry task
locator.quote: Open the [winning condition][def-wins] and find the clause

feedback.feedback: The concrete formal-inspection task is much better than a list of theorem names. Still, a student with no Lean experience needs to know that some (s h) represents a defined partial-function answer, not merely equality of two ordinary Boolean values. The linked definition’s English comment helps, but the relevant encoding is new.
feedback.why_it_matters: The reader may find the line without understanding why it simultaneously asserts promise membership and the value.
feedback.advice: Give a very small reading cue for the option-valued partial function, or direct the first-time reader to the record’s plain-language interpretation before asking for the clause. Keep the task optional to the mathematical proof.

locator.section: 7. The statement in Lean — precise scope
locator.quote: leaves the logarithmic power in the quantum bound unspecified

feedback.feedback: This is a useful and appropriately local explanation of the difference between the displayed family bound and the compared formal family theorem. It does not make readers wade through receipts to understand the difference.
feedback.why_it_matters: Formal checking of the headline result could otherwise be mistaken for a claim that every displayed explicit constant was compared in the same theorem.
feedback.advice: Keep this short scope sentence and the reminder to inspect definitions; do not expand the main exposition with execution metadata.

locator.quote: [long reasoning record](https://github.com/wcook04/quartic-query-lean/blob/main/docs/reasoning_record.md)

feedback.feedback: The introductory route uses the mutable main branch, while the section-specific proof links are pinned to c16d5d. I did not establish that the two currently disagree, but an assigned reading can later send students to two different editions of the same companion.
feedback.why_it_matters: Classroom references and example-reset warnings may stop matching after the public main branch changes.
feedback.advice: Resolve the overview and specific proof links to the same intended edition behind their ordinary readable link text. No visible hash is needed in the paper.
